# NASHA operating, kitchen, brewery, guest and digital-twin blueprint (generated by tools/blueprint_views.py; do not hand-edit)

**PROPOSED OPERATING MODEL - NOT FIELD VALIDATED. REQUIREMENTS FOR FUTURE PROFESSIONAL DESIGN - NOT A DESIGN. CONCEPTUAL / ILLUSTRATIVE - VISION MODEL, NOT ARCHITECTURAL APPROVAL.** Lane B (digital planning). Evidence stays 4/95 and design 43/95: digital work never raises physical evidence. No site, square footage, equipment brand, tank count, code compliance, permit or approval is claimed anywhere below. Agent-drafted from repository documents; no food-safety, alcohol-law, architectural or brewing professional has reviewed any of it.

## 1. Operating blueprint (PROPOSED OPERATING MODEL - NOT FIELD VALIDATED)

| Area | Proposed practice | Controls / checks | Owner role | Open question | Professional review required |

## 2. Kitchen blueprint (derived from the Core 5 menu)

| Element | Derived from | Requirement for a future architect or chef | Hazard / control | Open question | Professional |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Fryer station** | Chicken 65 Totopos (chicken and chips), possibly Gobi Taco | A fry position with separable oil handling for chicken, chips and any vegetarian fry | hot oil; water in oil; oil disposal; cross-contact of milk-containing marinade carryover into chip oil | Separate chip oil from chicken oil, or schedule them? | Food-safety professional; fire/hood professional |
| **Comal station** | Paneer Tikka Taco, Goat Birria, Gobi Taco, Butter Chicken & Roasted Poblano... | Dry flat-top or comal positions sized by the measured taco/quesadilla load; the likely shared bottleneck | burn risk; tortilla lard check at receiving (D-54) | How many positions does measured demand need? | Chef; ventilation engineer |
| **Char / tandoor question** | Paneer Tikka Taco; chicken for the quesadilla | Decide char source: tandoor, charbroiler, or oven/broiler; decide only after Session 2 comparison | combustion/ventilation; heavy equipment | Is a tandoor justified for one or two dishes? | Fire/hood professional; chef |
| **Braise and hot hold** | Goat Birria (large braise, consomme) | Cooling, holding and reheating route for a large braise as set by a food-safety professional | large-batch cooling and hot holding are the highest food-safety exposure | What cooling process and time/temperature limits apply? | Food-safety professional (required) |
| **Cold prep and assembly** | Salsa, slaw, pickled onion, crema, garnish; vegetarian dishes | Separate cold prep with its own sink access and tools | cross-contact between raw chicken and ready-to-eat items | Dedicated vegetarian prep surface? | Food-safety professional |
| **Pass** | All dishes | Plating and heat-lamp or hold-free pass sized by measured ticket times | holding time limits at the pass (chip crispness is a 10-minute problem) | How many plating positions? | Chef |
| **Cold storage** | Chicken, goat, paneer and dairy, produce, sauces | Walk-in or reach-in capacity derived from par levels measured in tests; raw proteins stored below ready-to-eat | temperature control; raw-over-ready-to-eat ordering | What par levels follow from real usage? | Food-safety professional |
| **Dry storage** | Flour, rice flour, cornflour, spices, dried chiles, oil | Dry shelving off the floor with labelling and allergen separation | pests; allergen labelling | none beyond measured par levels | Food-safety professional |
| **Freezer** | Tortillas if frozen, stocks, backup protein | Freezer capacity from measured needs | thaw procedure; labelling | Is freezing acceptable for tortillas and goat quality? | Chef; food-safety professional |
| **Receiving** | All supply | Receiving area with scale, thermometer, label check station, route that avoids crossing prep | D-54 label check (no beef, pork, lard, gelatin, isinglass); temperature at receipt | Delivery windows and docks unknown | Food-safety professional; architect |
| **Prep** | All dishes | Prep area sized by batch sizes proven in tests; raw-chicken prep zone separate from ready-to-eat | raw chicken contamination; knife and board separation | Prep volume per day is unknown | Chef; food-safety professional |
| **Handwashing** | All stations | Handwash sinks at prep, cook line, and dish entry | hand hygiene | Count and placement per local rule | Health authority via architect |
| **Dish** | All service | Dish area with route for dirty ware that does not cross the pass | cross-contamination; chemical storage | Machine vs manual question | Food-safety professional |
| **Waste** | Trim, spoiled product, oil, spent grain if brewery adjacent | Waste handling and grease/oil disposal route | pests; odor; grease | Oil collection arrangement unknown | Architect; plumbing engineer |
| **Allergen and cross-contact controls** | Milk (yogurt, crema, paneer), possible egg, corn, chile, sesame/mustard if... | Dedicated tools and cleaning routine; allergen matrix kept with the menu | cross-contact; mislabeling | Which dishes can be offered free of which allergens? | Food-safety professional; allergist advice for... |
| **Raw chicken flow** | Chicken 65, Butter Chicken Quesadilla | Raw chicken enters, is stored low, prepped in a marked zone and cooked to the required safe temperature without crossing ready-to-eat areas | cross-contamination; undercooking (safe core temperature is probed, never judged by eye) | Zone size and placement | Food-safety professional |
| **Vegetarian flow** | Paneer Tikka Taco, Gobi Taco | Vegetarian items handled on separate tools/surfaces; no beef/pork derivatives in any base (D-54) | hidden animal derivatives in stocks, fats, tortillas | Shared fryer for vegetarian and chicken items? | Food-safety professional |
| **Goat and dairy handling** | Goat Birria; paneer, yogurt, crema, cheese | Distinct storage and handling procedures for goat and dairy | spoilage; temperature abuse | Supplier cut specification unresolved | Food-safety professional |
| **Ventilation / hood questions** | Fryer, comal, char source | List cooking appliances and their ventilation needs for a professional | grease fire; air quality | Hood type and size are professional calls | Mechanical and fire professionals |
| **Oil handling** | Frying oil use measured in Session 1 | Filter, store, dispose of used oil per a professional's procedure | burns; fire; slip | Oil use per day is unknown until measured | Food-safety professional |

## 3. Brewery blueprint (requirements; tank size and count are NOT fixed)

| Element | What the future design must answer | Depends on | Scale sensitivity | Interaction with food and guests | Professional |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **pilot pathway** | Which route (collaboration, host residency, contract, own pilot) tests the Core 5 first, and what does each need from an attorney? | legal pathway; brewer availability | Low: decided before any vessel choice | Pairing tests with real food can run before any brewery space exists | Brewer; Texas alcohol attorney |
| **brew day workflow** | What sequence of tasks, people and movements does a brew day need, and what does it do to kitchen service hours? | scale; staffing; floor plan | High: grows with batch size and brews per week | Brew day heat, steam, noise and deliveries may collide with prep and service | Brewer; engineer |
| **fermentation** | How many fermenters, sized how, for five styles on rotation, dedicated or shared? The brewer answers; no count is assumed. | tank-turn analysis; style mix; brewer | Very high: central sizing question | Beer readiness must match menu and pairing calendar | Brewer |
| **conditioning and lagering** | Is lager a real need? If so, what cold-tank capacity and time does the brewer require without idle tanks? | style mix; fermentation; cold utilities | Very high: lager time strains small systems | Lager availability limits which dishes can be paired on launch | Brewer |
| **cold storage** | What beer and ingredient cold storage is needed, separate from food cold storage, and where does it sit? | kegging; packaging route; floor plan | Medium to high | Avoid competing with kitchen refrigeration, access and food-safety separation | Brewer; engineer; health-code reviewer |
| **kegging** | How are kegs filled, cleaned, stored, tracked and moved, and do kegs ever leave the building? | legal route; draft system; cold storage | Medium: depends on volume and outside sales | Keg traffic must avoid guest routes and food prep paths | Brewer; Texas alcohol attorney |
| **draft system** | What tap count, line layout, gas and balance approach and line-cleaning routine serve the beer list and seating? | tap count; taproom layout; gas supply | Medium: grows with tap count and distance | Bar placement, pour speed and server flow affect food service pacing | Brewer; draft specialist; engineer |
| **cleaning and CIP** | What cleaning approach, chemical handling, rinse capture and verification suit the equipment, and who runs it? | chemical storage; wastewater; scale | Medium to high: more vessels, more cleaning load | Cleaning chemicals and drains must stay away from food areas and guests | Brewer; engineer; safety reviewer |
| **water** | What water quantity, quality and treatment are needed for brewing, cleaning and cooling, and what utility data is missing? | site; utility data; scale | High: brewing uses far more than kitchen alone | Shared supply and pressure with kitchen, restrooms and cooling | Engineer; brewer; water-quality tester |
| **wastewater** | What load, temperature and solids will leave the brewery, and what do local sewer and pretreatment rules require? | sewer limits; scale; CIP | High: grows with batch size and cleaning | Brewery drains and kitchen grease drains need a plan for separation or sharing | Civil/plumbing engineer; local utility |
| **grain storage and handling** | How is grain received, stored, protected from pests and moisture, milled and moved, and where does dust go? | deliveries; scale; floor plan | High: bulk handling grows with scale | Dust and pests must stay away from food areas; allergen separation needs review | Brewer; engineer; food-safety reviewer |
| **chemical storage** | What chemicals are used, how are they segregated, labelled, contained and kept from food, guests and drains? | CIP; safety rules; floor plan | Medium | Never store near food, dry goods or guest routes; incompatible items kept apart | Safety professional; engineer; fire authority |
| **yeast handling** | Where are yeast sourced, stored, propagated or reused, and how is cross-contamination between styles avoided? | brewer; lab; style mix | Medium | Keep yeast and bread or fermentation work in the kitchen clearly separate | Brewer; lab professional |
| **QC and lab needs** | What checks (sensory, microbiological, analytical) does the brewer require, and what bench, space and records support them? | brewer; packaging route; scale | Medium: grows with outside sales | Sensory panels with food pairing need a clean, odour-controlled room | Brewer; lab professional |
| **cold room** | Is a walk-in cold room needed for kegs or ingredients, what size and location, and can it avoid sharing with food? | kegging; cold storage; floor plan | Medium to high | Separate from kitchen walk-ins unless a professional approves sharing | Brewer; engineer; health-code reviewer |
| **deliveries and receiving** | How do grain, hops, CO2, chemicals, kegs and food arrive and leave, and do routes conflict with guests? | site; loading access; schedule | Medium to high | Separate receiving routes or time windows from guest entry and kitchen deliveries | Architect; brewer; kitchen lead |
| **guest separation and safety** | How are guests kept apart from hot, wet, pressurised, chemical and moving-equipment areas, including any viewing? | floor plan; code review; scale | High: bigger production, bigger hazards | Guest viewing of brewing is a design choice that must not reduce safety or food hygiene | Architect; safety professional; code official |
| **food interaction: kitchen adjacency** | Should brewing sit next to the kitchen at all, and which flows (staff, ingredients, waste) would cross? | floor plan; kitchen layout | Medium | Adjacency may help staff and spent-grain reuse yet risks cross-contamination and congestion | Architect; chef; brewer |
| **food interaction: smells** | How will boil, grain and fermentation smells be kept from dining areas and from masking food aromas? | ventilation; floor plan; scale | Medium to high | Guest experience of food aromas depends on airflow separation | Mechanical engineer; architect |
| **food interaction: shared utilities** | Which utilities (water, drains, power, gas, cooling) are shared with the kitchen, and what can fail together? | utility design; scale | High | One utility failure could stop both brewing and service; capacity must be checked for both | Engineer; architect |
| **packaging question: kegs or cans** | Are kegs only, or cans also, wanted? Legal route comes first: what do Texas alcohol rules permit for this business? | legal route; sales plan; scale | Very high: cans may imply a different scale | Packaging space, noise and deliveries compete with dining space | Texas alcohol attorney; brewer |
| **spent grain** | Where is spent grain held, how is it removed, and may it be reused or must it be hauled away, given food-safety rules? | brewing scale; waste route; kitchen plan | High: volume follows batch size | Odour and pest control; any reuse in food needs professional review and allergen labelling | Brewer; food-safety reviewer; waste hauler |
| **utilities: power** | What electrical capacity, redundancy and distribution do brewing, cooling and lighting need beyond the kitchen? | scale; heat source; utility data | High | Peak loads may overlap with kitchen service | Electrical engineer; utility provider |
| **utilities: glycol** | Is a glycol chilling system needed, what loads does it serve, and where do the chiller and lines go? | fermentation; cold storage; scale | High: follows vessel count and cold-tank need | Mechanical noise and heat rejection must be kept from dining areas | Mechanical engineer; brewer |
| **utilities: steam or electric heat** | Should heating be steam, electric or another source, and what do fuel access, safety and local rules allow? | scale; fuel supply; code | High: affects every utility | Steam or gas uses can affect kitchen exhaust, supply and safety | Mechanical engineer; brewer; code official |
| **floor, drainage and floor loading** | What floor finish, slope, drain layout and structural loading do filled vessels and wet cleaning require? | vessel choice; structure; wastewater | Very high: filled tanks are heavy | Floor and drain details must keep wet brewery areas separate from food and guest areas | Structural engineer; architect; plumbing engineer |

## 4. Guest experience blueprint (PROPOSED - NOT FIELD VALIDATED)

| Stage | Guest goal | Design principle | Guest experiences | Staff behavior | Avoid | Recovery |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **DISCOVERY** | Learn what NASHA is and decide if it fits them. | Be honest and plain; show real work only; make no claim that is not yet true. | A clear page or sign that says what is offered, including the beer and non-alcoholic choices, without hype. | Answer questions truthfully and say what is not yet decided. | Exaggeration, borrowed culture, or implying awards or opinions that do not... | Correct any wrong information quickly and say so plainly. |
| **ARRIVAL** | Find the place and feel welcome without confusion. | Easy and obvious approach; no pressure; clear way in. | Clear wayfinding, shade where possible, and an entrance that is easy to read. | Greet people naturally as they appear; no scripted line. | Long waits in the sun, confusing entrances, loud hype. | Offer shade or a seat, explain the wait honestly, and update the guest. |
| **HOST** | Be acknowledged and told what happens next. | Honesty about wait and options. | A calm greeting, a straight answer on seating, and nothing to repeat if the guest chose to share a note ahead of time. | Make eye contact, answer directly, ask about access or allergen needs without drama. | Ignoring guests, wrong promises, bar queue blocking the host. | Apologise, give the honest next step, and ask a lead to help. |
| **SEATING** | Be placed comfortably where they can talk and see. | Choice and comfort; fit the party, not the system. | A table suited to the group, with access needs respected and noise considered. | Offer options rather than assign; seat families and mixed groups with care. | Forcing a table, awkward positions, seating near hazards. | Offer a move without fuss and thank the guest for saying. |
| **MENU** | Understand the food and drinks quickly. | Clarity first; allergens and dietary facts easy to find; vegetarian equal to the rest. | A readable menu with plain descriptions, allergen notes, and beer and non-alcoholic drinks given equal space. | Explain only if asked; know every dish and its allergens. | Jargon, buried allergen facts, unverified labels, halal or other claims not... | Admit when unsure, check with the kitchen, and tell the guest what is known. |
| **FOOD DISCOVERY** | Find dishes they will enjoy, whether vegetarian or not. | Curiosity without lectures; honest descriptions. | Dishes explained plainly, with the Indian and Mexican threads described with facts a source supports. | Describe food as cooks do, in simple words; offer suggestions, not pushes. | Performed culture, stories made up, pressure to order more. | Offer an alternative dish and note the preference for the kitchen. |
| **BEER / NA DISCOVERY** | Choose a drink they like, alcoholic or not, with equal... | Non-alcoholic choices stand level with beer in list, glass and care. | A drink list where non-alcoholic items are as considered as beer, with tasting help offered. | Ask what they like, offer small tastes where permitted, never push volume. | Treating non-alcoholic as a lesser option, or encouraging fast drinking. | Swap the drink without comment and note what was disliked. |
| **PAIRING** | See how food and drink go together if they want it. | Suggestion, not instruction; no medical or intoxication claims. | Optional suggestions for beer or non-alcoholic drinks, framed as ideas. | Offer a pairing only when interested; suggest both alcoholic and non-alcoholic options. | Scripts, forced pairing flights, tying alcohol to spice or heat as a challenge. | Replace the pairing freely and thank the guest for the feedback. |
| **SERVICE** | Receive food and drink at a natural pace with attention. | Attentive and unhurried; roles clear. | Food arrives in a sensible order, hot items hot and chips crisp, and staff notice needs. | Check in with care, read the table, and carry plates with the allergen note. | Long gaps, cold food, interrupting, plates forgotten. | Apologise, tell the guest the truth about delay, and remake or replace when... |
| **TABLE EXPERIENCE** | Enjoy time with their group in comfort. | Warm, social, and low-pressure; the table is theirs. | A clean table, water offered, and room to share food. | Clear in good time, refill water, and leave guests alone when they want. | Rushing guests out, constant interruption, mess left too long. | Fix the table, apologise briefly, and move on. |
| **PAYMENT** | Pay without friction or surprise. | Transparent and simple; no pressure on tips or extras. | A bill that is clear, with split options and no hidden items. | Bring the bill when asked or at a natural point; explain charges plainly. | Surprise charges, slow payment, pushing more drinks. | Correct errors immediately and fully, and apologise. |
| **DEPARTURE** | Leave feeling looked after and safe. | A warm close without scripted lines; guest safety comes first. | A simple thank you, easy exit, and information on safe travel options if needed. | Notice how guests are doing, offer water or a ride option where concerned, and thank them. | Ignoring a guest who is unwell, pressure to leave a review. | Involve a lead and help the guest get home safely. |
| **RETURN** | Want to come back because it was good, not because they... | Earn the return through quality and respect; no tricks. | A memory of good food, fair treatment, and equal choice of drinks. | Remember preferences if the guest agrees; do not fake familiarity. | Pushy loyalty schemes, invented regulars, pressure to return. | Invite feedback quietly and act on what is said. |
| **FAMILY EXPERIENCE** | Bring children comfortably while adults are respected. | Family welcome within rules; children kept apart from alcohol service as the rules require. | Kid-friendly choices that follow the no-beef, no-pork policy, high chairs if provided, and a calm table. | Be friendly, quick with children's food, and aware of alcohol near minors. | Treating families as a nuisance, alcohol near children, unsafe spots. | Move the table, speed the food, and ask a lead to help. |
| **ACCESSIBILITY INTENT** | Enter, move, order and eat with dignity. | Design intent only: no claim of code compliance; qualified professionals decide. | Clear paths, seating options, readable menus, and willingness to adapt. | Ask what would help, listen, and act without fuss or attention. | Assuming needs, blocked paths, loud speech about disability. | Fix it at once, apologise, and report the barrier to the manager. |
| **MUSIC AND LIGHTING** | Talk easily and feel at ease. | Warm, low-glare light and music that never overpowers conversation. | Light that suits eating and reading, and sound that allows talk. | Adjust to the room and guest comment; no staff taste imposed. | Club-like volume, harsh glare, themed stereotypes. | Lower the sound or change the light when a guest asks. |
| **TABLEWARE AND GLASSWARE** | Eat and drink from clean, sensible, comfortable ware. | Function over show; same care for non-alcoholic glassware as for beer glasses. | Clean plates and glasses suited to the food and drink, with no chipped items. | Check ware before service, replace damaged pieces, and handle glass safely. | Chipped or dirty ware, glass shortages, costume-like props. | Replace at once, apologise, and remove the damaged piece. |
| **PATIO** | Enjoy outdoor space in comfort and safety. | Shade, comfort, clear service path, respect for neighbours. | Seating with shade where possible, hot food timed carefully, and noise kept considerate. | Check tables regularly, bring water, and watch for weather changes. | Guests forgotten outside, food going cold, rowdy behaviour. | Bring a lead, relocate the guest if needed, and replace food that went cold. |

## 5. Architectural digital twin (CONCEPTUAL / ILLUSTRATIVE)

| Space | Intent | Adjacency and flow | Day vs night | Family / accessibility intent | Must not be claimed |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Exterior** | A warm, shaded, readable arrival that signals craft hospitality, not theme | Street or lot to entrance; patio visible | Daylight shade; evening warm light | Clear step-free approach intended | No site, no address, no approved sign |
| **Entrance** | A clear threshold with a welcome point and a view of the room and brewery glass | To host, bar, and dining without a bottleneck | Daytime easy entry; evening orderly entry | Door and threshold designed for step-free passage as an intent | No accessibility compliance claim |
| **Bar** | A social hub for beer and NA on equal footing, with the brewery visible | Near entrance; separate from the kitchen pass | Day: calm service; night: livelier but conversational | Part of the bar usable seated at an accessible height as an intent | No tap count, no equipment |

| **Storage** | Dry, cold and freezer storage placed to shorten kitchen trips | Receiving to storage to prep | n/a | n/a | No capacity |
| **Staff area** | Space for breaks, lockers, handwash, and training | Off back-of-house | n/a | Accessible to staff with disabilities intent | No code claim |

| **BAR-LED** | Bar is the social center; drinks lead, food follows. | Depends on bar skill; unknown. | Unknown: bar bottleneck risk at peak. | Strong for beer and NA discovery; weaker for food order. | Weaker if bar is the focus and alcohol is central; needs separation. | Unknown; beer sales may rise but food mix may suffer. | Medium: guests lean on bartenders for choices. | Medium: bar must handle food runner links. | Does a bar-led format hurt family comfort or food-first identity? |
| **TABLE SERVICE WITH FAST CORE** | High on tables with a quick core menu to protect the chip. | Medium-high: floor staff plus a stable fast line; unknown. | Likely better for dishes with short hold windows; unproven. | Strong: simple core menu eases pairing guidance. | Strong: quick children's items and a calm table. | Unknown; could rise with pairing but menu is limited. | Medium: guest chooses but core is fixed. | Medium: tight menu helps; two speed lanes complicate. | Does a fast core menu protect quality at tables and still feel... |

| **brunch** | Beer is optional; NA and light styles matter more. | Some dishes could adapt; others may not fit brunch habits. | Adds a separate prep and menu set. | Possible brunch-only items; risk to the Core 5 focus. | Weekend staffing pattern; unknown. | Could pull NASHA toward a generic brunch identity. | Does brunch demand exist, and does it fit the Indian-Mexican idea? |

| **weekend** | Beer sales and visitors likely higher; patio matters. | Full menu likely; kitchen pressure high. | Peaks strain every system. | Possible weekend specials; unproven. | Highest staffing pressure; unknown. | Can raise visibility but risks hurting quality and family comfort. | Do weekends justify full hours, and what peak plan protects quality? |

## 14. Sustainability and resource use (measure first, improve later; no promises)

| Topic | Material operational question | Measure first | Later improvement question |
|---|---|---|---|
| **water** | Where does water enter and leave the kitchen, brewery and restrooms, and which uses are largest? | Meter or log water use by area during a pilot. | Which uses can be reduced without hurting safety or quality? |
| **brewery wastewater** | What does brewery wastewater contain and where does it go? | Record volumes and basic character with the brewer and utility. | What handling changes are possible if the utility or engineer advises them? |
| **spent grain** | Where does spent grain go after each brew and who can take it? | Track amounts and destinations of grain for a pilot period. | Is there a dependable, safe outlet worth arranging? |
| **cooking oil** | How much fry oil is used, how long does it last, and how is it disposed of? | Log oil changes and the disposal route. | Could filtering, scheduling or a collector reduce use? |
| **food waste** | What food is thrown away, at which stage, and why? | Weigh and log waste by category during tests and early service. | Which menu, prep or portion changes address the biggest sources? |
| **packaging** | What packaging comes in and goes out, and which is single-use? | List packaging by item and supplier during pilot purchasing. | Can suppliers, formats or reusable options change without harming food safety? |
| **energy** | Which equipment drives energy use, such as fryers, cold rooms and brewing heat? | Read meters or bills by area where possible. | Which efficiency or scheduling steps are worth studying with an engineer? |
| **refrigeration** | How much cold storage is needed and how well is it kept cold and sealed? | Log temperatures, door habits and equipment condition. | Would layout, maintenance or sizing changes cut waste and energy? |
| **local sourcing where economically sensible** | Which ingredients can be sourced nearby at workable quality and price? | Track supplier origin, price and reliability for pilot items. | Which local relationships are worth deepening, given cost and consistency? |
| **reuse and recycling** | What can be reused or recycled in practice with local services? | Sort and observe what is actually collected and contaminated. | Which streams are worth the staff time and space? |

## 15. Safety and incident planning (planning level; professional safety planning required)

| Hazard | Where it arises | Planning control idea | Professional requirement | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **burns** | Comal, fryer, oven, hot braise and hot liquids in the kitchen | Defined hot zones, protective gear, clear calling of hot items, first aid on hand | Safety consultant and fire professional; local authority. Planning level only; not a... | Kitchen lead |
| **cuts** | Prep stations, slicers, knives and broken ware | Training, sharp tools kept sharp, cut-resistant gear and a stated clean-up process | Safety consultant and food-safety professional | Kitchen lead |
| **hot oil** | Fryer station, oil filtering and disposal, water near oil | Trained handling, cooling before moving oil, no water near oil, fire suppression at the hood | Fire professional, hood designer and safety consultant | Kitchen lead |
| **slips** | Wet kitchen and brewery floors, bar spills, patio rain, entrances | Footwear rules, drainage, mats, prompt spill clean-up, visible wet-floor warnings | Safety consultant and architect | General manager |
| **chemical handling** | Cleaning and sanitizing chemicals in kitchen and brewery | Labelled containers, separated storage, training, safety data sheets on hand and eye wash planned | Safety consultant, brewer and food-safety professional | Brewer and kitchen lead |
| **CO2** | Cylinders, bulk gas, fermentation areas, cold rooms and keg handling | Ventilation, detection and alarm planning, secured cylinders, trained handling, restricted access | Mechanical engineer, gas supplier, fire professional and safety consultant | Brewer |
| **brewery confined-space hazards** | Entry into tanks, vessels and pits | Entry prohibited by default, written permit approach, two-person rule, rescue planning | Safety consultant and brewer; authority guidance; not self-designed | Brewer |
| **glass breakage** | Bar, dining room, bottle handling, recycling and patio | Break-handling steps, safer ware where suitable, covered bins and a quick clean-up routine | Insurance broker and safety consultant | Bar lead |
| **intoxication** | Bar and table service of beer | Responsible-alcohol practices, hydration and food, calm refusals, rideshare help, staff training | Texas alcohol attorney, insurance broker and approved server training | General manager |
| **guest incidents** | Falls, allergic reactions, injuries, disputes and medical events | Incident log, staff roles, first aid, calls to emergency services, post-event reviews | Insurance broker, attorney and safety consultant | General manager |
| **fire** | Hood and fryer, gas equipment, electrical, brewery heat and dining areas | Egress planning, extinguishers, drills, clean hood and vents, defined shutoffs | Fire professional, fire marshal and insurance broker | General manager |
| **severe weather** | Storms, flooding, heat and cold affecting patio, supply and safety | Weather watching, patio closure triggers, shelter plan, secured outdoor items | Safety consultant and insurance broker; emergency management guidance | General manager |
| **power outage** | Loss of power to cold storage, lights, POS and brewing | Backup lighting, cold-hold discipline, safe shutdown of fryers and equipment | Electrician, fire professional and food-safety professional | General manager and kitchen lead |

## 16. Continuity questions (lightweight)

| Scenario | Immediate conceptual response | Resilience requirement | Dependency | Professional |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **refrigeration fails** | Keep doors shut, check temperatures, move food to working cold space, stop using at-risk items, tell the lead. | Written hold-or-discard decisions set by a professional; monitoring and service contacts. | Maintenance service, cold storage, food-safety professional | Food-safety professional |
| **POS fails** | Switch to a manual order and payment routine; keep a paper list; reconcile once it recovers. | Offline plan, backup pad and paper, trained staff. | POS provider, payment processor, network | Accountant and operations advisor |
| **water fails** | Pause water-dependent work; use bottled water for essentials; decide whether food service can safely continue. | Written closure triggers and handwashing and sanitation rules set by authorities. | Utility, plumbing, health authority | Food-safety professional and health authority |
| **power fails** | Protect cold items, stop fryers safely, use backup light, decide whether to continue or close. | Safe shutdown steps, backup lighting, cold-hold discipline. | Utility, electrician, backup power supplier | Fire and food-safety professionals |
| **supplier misses delivery** | Use alternates, simplify the menu, or sell out of affected items honestly. | Second supplier option, ordering buffer, clear substitution rules that respect D-54. | Suppliers, distributors, receiving process | Chef and operations advisor |
| **beer system fails** | Offer bottles or cans if available, non-alcoholic choices, or other draft lines; tell guests plainly. | Backup serving plan, maintenance contacts, trained staff. | Brewer, draft engineer, gas supplier | Brewer and safety consultant |
| **one Core dish becomes unavailable** | Remove it from the menu, offer a simple alternate, and keep pairings honest. | Defined fallback dishes and menu update routine; no unapproved substitutions. | Suppliers, kitchen, menu process | Chef |
| **key employee calls out** | Reassign tasks, simplify service, call in cross-trained staff, or reduce the menu. | Cross-training and written station guides; no invented staffing counts. | Staffing plan, labor attorney for questions | Employment attorney and accountant |

## 18. Operating collision map (updated; none solved)

**COLLISION TO MEASURE - NOT SOLVED**

| Collision | Where | Why it matters | What a future test measures |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Fryer peak with comal peak** | Kitchen during busy meals when chips, fried items, tacos and quesadillas fire together | Two stations peak at once and a short pass cannot plate both while fried items stay crisp | Order-to-plate time and chip crispness when fryer and comal tickets overlap |
| **NA garnish with bar peak** | Bar when beer pours and garnished NA drinks are ordered together | Cut citrus and herb garnish adds bar steps and can make the NA drink slower than beer | Pour-and-garnish time for NA versus beer when queued together |
| **Pairing explanation with table turns** | Table service when guests ask for pairings | Explaining pairings takes server time that competes with turning tables and with attention to other guests | Server minutes per pairing conversation and whether it delays seating or service |
| **Beer glass complexity with dishwashing** | Glass wash and bar when many glass shapes are in use | More shapes increase wash handling, breakage and shortage risk, and NA glassware needs equal care | Glass turn time and shortages with different shape counts |
| **Goat prep with cold storage** | Cold room and walk-in during braise cooling and raw goat storage | Cooling a large braise can displace other stock, and raw goat must stay separate from ready food | Cooling time and cold-space use of a braise beside normal stock |
| **Family traffic with brewery visibility** | Entrance and dining where children and alcohol production or service share sightlines | Families need a comfortable table while alcohol service stays apart as rules require | Family routes against bar and brewhouse sightlines; an attorney sets the rules |
| **Raw protein with vegetarian prep** | Prep stations and fryer where chicken and goat are near paneer and gobi | Vegetarian guests expect separation and allergens must not cross | Cross-contact risk points in station layout and shared fryer oil |
| **Shared comal across tortilla warming, quesadilla and goat tacos** | Comal bank near the pass | One heat surface is the assumed bottleneck for three Core 5 dishes | Comal minutes per plate and queue length with mixed orders |
| **Dipped goat tacos with consomme service** | Pass and table for the goat dish | Hot consomme cups add plating steps and a spill and burn risk for tables with children | Plate time, spill points and temperature on arrival |
| **Dairy cold chain for a lassi-style NA drink** | Walk-in and bar for cultured dairy used in the quesadilla pairing | Cold shelf competes with kitchen dairy and the drink shortens the pairing list if it fails | Cold shelf space and shelf-life limits of the drink |
| **Dish pit load of pots, plates and glasses** | Dish area after braise, sauce and service | Pots and glasses compete for one wash path and wash time | Wash cycle time when braise pots and glasses arrive together |
| **Closing cooldown with next-day prep** | Kitchen at close with braise, makhani and marinades | Cooling and labelling compete with cleaning and prep for the next day | Cooldown and labelling time at close |
| **Patio distance with chip crispness** | Patio service route | Chips lose crunch during a long carry, and patio guests are easy to forget | Crispness after the patio carry and patio plate delay |

## 19. Adjacency requirements (for a future architect)

| Pair | Relation | Why | Open question |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Kitchen pass and dining** | MUST be close | Food reaches the table before chips lose crispness | How many pass positions and where |
| **Fryer and comal stations** | SHOULD be near the pass; MUST be separable from each other | Different heat and hazard profiles; collision at peak | Whether one hood or two |
| **Raw chicken prep and ready-to-eat assembly** | MUST be separated | Cross-contamination control | Zone sizes by a food-safety professional |
| **Bar and kitchen pass** | SHOULD be close but not sharing a path | Shared service staff while keeping drink and food flows apart | Pickup and runner paths |
| **Brewery and dining** | SHOULD be visible; MUST be separated for guest safety | Brewing in plain sight without hazard exposure | Glass, rails, floor drainage |
| **Brewery and kitchen** | SHOULD share utilities where sensible; MUST not share food flow | Heat, steam and chemical separation from food | Utility adjacency decisions |
| **Receiving and storage** | MUST be close; MUST avoid guest routes | Deliveries and spoilage control | Dock and route |
| **Family seating and the bar** | SHOULD be apart | Adult-focused bar and responsible-alcohol design | Policy and legal view on minors |
| **Patio and kitchen pass** | SHOULD have a short runner path | Heat and distance degrade food | Patio service station |
| **Dish area and pass** | AVOID crossing | Dirty ware crossing clean flow | Layout |

### Site deal-breakers and the walk-away rule

Deal-breaker candidates in the site scorecard: Grease and ventilation (hood), Zoning and brewery use, Alcohol licence pathway fit, ADA and accessibility. Rule (proposed): while any deal-breaker is unknown at decision time, the site decision is HOLD, never a guess. No site has been identified.


## 20. Technology needs (no vendors, no prices)

| Function | Need class | Why | MVP alternative without a vendor | Decision trigger |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **POS** | ESSENTIAL AT FLAGSHIP | A venue taking orders daily needs one; early tests are small and handled by hand. | Manual order tally and a basic payment method permitted by the event rules | Regular public sales begin |
| **KDS** | TOO EARLY | Kitchen display matters only with enough tickets to coordinate stations. | Paper tickets and a call-out | Ticket volume overwhelms paper at a real site |
| **inventory** | ESSENTIAL AT FLAGSHIP | Food and brewing stock need tracking once volume and waste matter. | Spreadsheet from receipts and counts | Recurring weekly purchasing |
| **recipe costing** | ESSENTIAL AT MVP | Cost per portion is the core unknown; needed from Session 1. | Spreadsheet using receipts, weights and yields | Already needed |
| **reservations and waitlist** | OPTIONAL | Useful for seated service; ticketed tastings can use simple lists. | Simple sign-up list for invited tastings | Seated service with variable demand |
| **labor scheduling** | TOO EARLY | Few or no staff during validation. | Shared calendar with helpers | Regular paid staff |
| **accounting** | ESSENTIAL AT MVP | Any paid event needs clean records and separate money. | Spreadsheet of receipts and sales | First paid event |
| **payroll** | TOO EARLY | No employees yet. | None needed | First paid employee |
| **website** | ESSENTIAL AT MVP | Presents the evidence and process; the private site already exists. | The existing static private site | Public launch decision |
| **analytics** | OPTIONAL | Early learning comes from tasting sheets, not traffic data. | Tasting forms and manual counts | Public site with real traffic |
| **CRM and loyalty** | TOO EARLY | No customers; loyalty needs repeat guests. | Opt-in contact list for test invitees | Repeat attendance appears |
| **guest feedback** | ESSENTIAL AT MVP | Scores and comments from tasters are the main evidence. | Paper or simple form with frozen questions | Already needed |
| **Wi-Fi and network** | ESSENTIAL AT FLAGSHIP | Needed for payments and systems in a fixed venue. | Phone data connection at events | A fixed site exists |
| **security** | ESSENTIAL AT FLAGSHIP | A fixed venue holding stock, cash and data needs protection. | Basic habits at tests; no stored card data | A fixed site exists |
| **backup** | ESSENTIAL AT MVP | Records and evidence are the asset today and must not be lost. | Copies on separate storage | Already needed |
| **brewery tracking** | ESSENTIAL AT FLAGSHIP | Batch, tank and compliance records are required once brewing starts. | Brewer's logbook in a pilot or host brewery | Brewing on own equipment |
